presentingComplaint: Reduced urine output, muscle cramps, and nausea/vomiting on day 2 after induction chemotherapy for high-grade B-cell lymphoma.
history: 52-year-old man with newly diagnosed high-grade B-cell lymphoma (bulky abdominal disease, high LDH at baseline) received the first cycle of R-CHOP-type induction chemotherapy 48 hours ago. He now reports decreased urine output over the last 12 hours, generalized muscle cramps, paraesthesiae around the mouth and fingertips, nausea with two episodes of vomiting, and mild lethargy. No fever reported by the patient. No prior renal disease. Received allopurinol prophylaxis but chemotherapy was started urgently given bulky, rapidly proliferating disease and adequate hydration was reportedly suboptimal in the first 24 hours (intermittent IV fluids, no formal urine output charting).
examination: Alert but mildly drowsy, oriented. No rash. Mild bilateral lower limb oedema. Chvostek sign equivocal. Abdomen: palpable bulky non-tender mass in the epigastrium/left upper quadrant consistent with known lymphomatous disease; no peritonism. No cardiac gallop. Reduced urine output noted on catheter bag (oliguric).

labs.ecg: peaked T waves, widened QRS, borderline PR prolongation

imaging: Renal ultrasound: normal-sized kidneys, no hydronephrosis, no evidence of obstructive uropathy
Abdominal CT (pre-chemo staging): bulky retroperitoneal and mesenteric lymphadenopathy with large tumour burden
differentialDiagnoses: Acute kidney injury from other cause (contrast nephropathy, obstructive uropathy)
Chemotherapy-induced acute kidney injury (e.g., methotrexate nephrotoxicity if applicable)

finalDiagnosis: Tumour lysis syndrome (laboratory and clinical TLS per Cairo-Bishop criteria) with acute kidney injury, hyperkalemia, hyperuricemia, hyperphosphatemia, and hypocalcemia post-induction chemotherapy for high-grade lymphoma
citations: Harrison 22e — Oncologic Emergencies: Tumor Lysis Syndrome
ASCO/Cairo-Bishop Tumor Lysis Syndrome Guideline 2008 (updated consensus)
contraindications: Avoid rasburicase in G6PD deficiency (risk of hemolysis) — screen before use in at-risk populations
Avoid potassium-containing or lactate-containing IV fluids in hyperkalemia
Avoid correcting hypocalcemia unless symptomatic (tetany, seizures, arrhythmia) due to risk of precipitating calcium phosphate deposition given concurrent hyperphosphatemia
Alkalinized fluids are not routinely recommended and may worsen calcium-phosphate precipitation
edgeCases: Tumour lysis syndrome is not present as a distinct diagnosable id in the current disease vocabulary; closest overlapping engine concepts are hyperkalemia and aki, but neither captures the composite Cairo-Bishop syndrome, so acceptableIds is set to [] per rules

Clinical TLS (with AKI, arrhythmia risk, or seizure) requires urgent nephrology involvement and consideration of renal replacement therapy if refractory hyperkalemia, severe acidosis, oliguria/anuria, or symptomatic hypocalcemia develop
High LDH and bulky, rapidly proliferating disease (as here) are recognized high-risk features for TLS independent of baseline renal function
Rasburicase preferred over allopurinol once hyperuricemia is established, but was not used here initially — a clinically relevant management gap to flag
expectedMaiK: MaiK should flag this as an oncologic emergency (tumour lysis syndrome) rather than an infective/sepsis picture — highlighting the temporal link to chemotherapy, the composite metabolic derangement (hyperkalemia, hyperuricemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia) with AKI, and the need for urgent correction of hyperkalemia, aggressive IV hydration, urate-lowering therapy (rasburicase), and nephrology/ICU involvement with low threshold for dialysis.
expectedNextQuestions: Was rasburicase given or only allopurinol, and is G6PD status known?
What is the current urine output over the last 6 hours (oliguria/anuria)?
Is there ECG evidence of hyperkalemia-related conduction abnormality requiring emergent stabilization (calcium gluconate, insulin-dextrose)?
Is the patient symptomatic from hypocalcemia (tetany, seizure, QT prolongation)?
Has nephrology been consulted regarding need for urgent hemodialysis?
What was the baseline tumour burden/LDH and was TLS risk stratified before chemotherapy?

Renal ultrasound to exclude obstructive cause

G6PD screen if rasburicase being considered
